title: Teachings I've Appreciated
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley shares teachings drawn from recorded talks online, starting with Gil Fransdell's daily question, "If this was the last day of my life, how would I like to spend it?", and Shodo Hirata Roshi's poem "In This Passing Moment." Seishu recalls a month of post-surgery rest that went better once the complaining stopped, and reads Karen Armstrong's description of nirvana as an inner haven in the midst of pain. Two more teachings follow: the path is always a step away, and Zen forms introduce us to limits. Seishu then turns to Gloria Steinem's evening at the Mount Baker Theatre, where "linked, not ranked" and small daily kindnesses echo sangha, Dogen, and Suzuki Roshi's "shining one corner of the world." Seishu ends with the three pieces of advice Norman Fischer gives new priests: be humble, see everyone as Buddha, try to be helpful.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody, and welcome.
For most of the years that I've been practicing, I almost never listened to dharma talks online.
Once in a while, if I heard a good talk here or at Samish Island, I might listen to it again at home, but that was pretty rare.
In the last couple months, I'm not sure why I decided this, but I've been listening to dharma talks probably four or five times a week, and I've really been enjoying it and getting a lot out of it.
On the Everyday Zen website I've been listening to talks by Norman Fischer and Kathy Fischer.
I've been listening to Gil Fransdell.
He, like Norman, is a dharma heir of Sojun Mel Weitsman, although maybe 10 or 12 years ago he started to teach in the Vipassana tradition.
He's got hundreds of talks online.
And I've been listening to Jack Duffy.
He lives in Whatcom County here, and he's a dharma heir of Robert Aitken.
Most of his talks are about koans, so they're full of dialogues between Chinese and Japanese teachers and students.
Very interesting.
And there are talks on the Upaya Zen Center website.
It's almost overwhelming, the number of dharma talks that are available online, but it's been a great resource.
What I thought I would do tonight is just share with you some of the things I've heard in the different teachings that I've most appreciated.
In one of Gil Fransdell's talks he described an exercise that he did every day for a year.
He would ask himself every morning, "If this was the last day of my life, how would I like to spend it?"
I thought, well, that's a really good question, and I thought I would try that myself.
So for about the last month, most days, I asked myself that question.
Once in a while I forget, but when I remember and I ask that question, it really focuses me: what do I want to do right now, or what's important right now?
There's really not much confusion.
One thing that has been coming up is that I want to make sure the people I love know that.
So I spend time with my wife and I let her know how I feel, and I let my daughter know how I feel, and I've been doing that.
Before I was asking this question, I would think, oh, I should give my daughter a call and tell her this or that, and I meant to do that, but then days would go by and I wouldn't do it.
With this exercise I'm not putting it off, because you never know how much time you have left to spend with the people you really care about.
It's quite a reminder of that.
The other thing I've noticed is that I'm even more careful with how I spend my time.
I've been pretty good about that anyway.

A lot of times at the end of the day I'll review the choices I made, and usually I'm pretty happy with them, but with this question I'm even less likely to just get on the computer and look at this and that, or turn on the television.
So it's really been a good exercise for thinking about how you want to use your time.
I recommend that you give this question a try, even if you did it for a week.

Another talk that I listened to had to do with saying yes to what is, and that there is a freedom in choosing to accept a situation that you don't have any choice about, especially a difficult situation, that there's less suffering if you choose to accept it.
That means you acknowledge what's happening, you turn towards it, you allow it to be there, and then you try to respond in the best possible way.
In this particular talk there was a poem by Shodo Hirata Roshi.
I hadn't heard of him.
He's a Japanese Rinzai priest, born in 1940, and he's still alive.
He's the abbot of the Sogenji temple in Okayama, Japan, but he also founded the One Drop Zen monastery on Whidbey Island, not far from here.
His poem is called "In This Passing Moment."
*In this passing moment karma ripens and all things come to be.
I vow to choose what is.
If there is cost, I choose to pay.
If there is need, I choose to give.
If there is pain, I choose to feel.
If there is sorrow, I choose to grieve.
When burning, I choose heat.
When calm, I choose peace.
When starving, I choose hunger.
When happy, I choose joy.
Whom I encounter, I choose to meet.
What I shoulder, I choose to bear.
When it is my death, I choose to die.
Where this takes me, I choose to go.
Being with what is, I respond to what is.
This life is as real as a dream.
The one who knows it cannot be found, and truth is not a thing.
Therefore I vow to choose this Dharma entrance gate.
May all Buddhas and wise ones help me live this vow.*
A few years ago I had a minor surgery, and my instructions afterward from the doctor were to avoid all physical exertion for a month.
He said even be careful going up the stairs.
I don't like that.
I like to be active, I like to move around, and I really didn't like those instructions.
I remember coming home, and it was early October.
I was standing in my living room and I looked out the window and saw people, it was 70 degrees out there, riding their bikes and walking their dogs and jogging by.
I thought, I don't like this, I don't want to sit here for a month and do nothing.
I spent about five minutes complaining to myself, and then I thought, whoa, if you keep this up you're gonna have a really, really bad month, and you're gonna drive your wife nuts.
So I said to myself, I just have to accept it, I have to make the best of it, which I did.
I thought, okay, I better get some books, I better figure out some things to do that I can do sitting down.
The month went pretty well.
I missed doing the things that I would have done otherwise, but I got by pretty well, much better because I did stop complaining.

My wife has had a number of big surgeries, knee replacements, rotator cuff surgery, and she's really good at just going through what she has to go through, doing the rehab, no complaining, a really good attitude.
So she's a very good role model for me.
This poem reminds me of one of my favorite passages from a book called *Buddha* by Karen Armstrong.
She's a religious writer.
She was a nun for 12 or 13 years and then left whatever the order she was in, and has just been writing about religion ever since.
This is a biography of the Buddha, but it has quite a bit about Buddhist practice, so I want to read you a section from that.
*The attainment of Nirvana did not mean that the Buddha would never experience any more suffering.
He would grow old, get sick and die like everybody else, and would experience pain while doing so.

Nirvana does not give an awakened trance-like immunity, but an inner haven which enables a man or a woman to live with pain, to take possession of it, affirm it, and experience a profound peace of mind in the midst of suffering.
Nirvana, therefore, is found within oneself, in the very heart of each person's being.
It's an entirely natural state.
It is not bestowed by grace nor achieved for us by a supernatural savior.
It can be reached by anybody who cultivates the path as assiduously as the Buddha did.
Nirvana is a still center.
It gives meaning to life.*
I really think this is the same thing that Hirata Roshi was talking about in his poem, experiencing difficulty with acceptance.
It's not an easy thing to do.

It's our nature to want to avoid or deny or resist the things that we don't want, but each one of us can experiment and see if we have less suffering by accepting the things that we don't have a choice about.
I just want to make it clear that acceptance is not a passive experience.
It's not "oh well, there's nothing I can do."
It's fully experiencing what you're going through, and it's also thinking about what's the best way to respond.
But it's not adding things like "I hate this," "this shouldn't be happening," "why is this happening," "this isn't fair," all the things we can add to a difficult experience to make it worse.
Another talk that I listened to, changing subjects, was on staying on the path of practice.
What was mentioned in this talk is that once you decide to practice the path and you really make a commitment to it, it's always right by your side, it's right next to you.

Even if you go off the path, which we all do from time to time for the usual reasons, I'm too busy, maybe I have some doubts whether I ought to be doing this, whether it's worth doing, maybe laziness, or a whole bunch of life events get in the way, the path is always a step away.
So whenever you decide to come back, you can just step right back on, and you don't have to bring any guilt with you.
You can just set that down, step back on the path, and the path is always glad to have you back.
I like that part.
It's like a lifetime membership that never expires, so even if you take a break, you can come right back.
Another one of the talks touched on the topic of forms in Zen.
We have a lot of them.
I think some of you might be here for the first time, but we bow, we chant, we have a way that the zendo is organized.
We have a very definite schedule: meditation starts, and then there's walking meditation.
We have very specific postures to sit in when you're meditating or to walk in when you're doing walking meditation.
I've always liked the explanation that the forms are mindfulness exercises.
They help us pay attention, and once you have a basic understanding of them you don't have to think about what to do or when to do it or how to do it.
It's all laid out for you, and that actually helps you have a much deeper meditation experience.
I've certainly found that to be the case.
But this talk mentioned something different that I had never thought of before.
What they talked about was that part of Zen practice is to intentionally introduce you to limits.
If we're in a residential meditation retreat, you get up at a certain time, you come to the meditation hall at a certain time, you sit, you walk, you take breaks at a certain time.
None of this is of your choosing.
So Zen intentionally puts you up against limits, and then you get a chance to watch how your body and how your mind responds to limits, and what's the best way to respond to limitation.
The value of that is that we run into so many limitations in our day-to-day life.
I don't have enough money, I don't have enough time, I'm in a traffic jam, I have a health problem.
It's really valuable to have some experience and some skill at learning what's the best way to respond to a limitation.
So I like that explanation for one of the advantages of the forms, which sometimes, but they can be useful.
Then there's one other thing I wanted to mention.
This is a little bit of a change of topic, but it's relevant to practice.
At the end of November my wife and I went to hear Gloria Steinem at the Mount Baker Theatre.
Did anybody here see her?
You did, okay.
It was great.
She was there for an hour and a half and she was interviewed by someone on the stage.
Does anybody not know who she is?
Okay.
She's 85 years old, and she's been an activist for women's rights, reproductive rights, probably for 60 years.
She's written books, she founded *Ms.* magazine.
She's one of these rare people who's been an activist, in the front lines, for all of her life.
So it was a real privilege to see her.
The place was packed, which is great, it was sold out, with a lot of younger people in their 30s and 40s, which I found encouraging.
A couple things really stood out for me.
She had lots of energy.
Usually some people who are 85, for good reason, are a little tired, and you can see that, but for an hour and a half she just had plenty of energy.
Even though she talked about difficult topics, reproductive rights, domestic violence, politics, women's rights, she just maintained equanimity the whole time.
She had a lot of calmness about her, which is rare when you're talking about these kinds of topics.
Then she said a number of things that I thought were really in accord with our practice, so I just wanted to go over a couple of them.
One of the things she mentioned is that if you're gonna be an activist, you have to have a support group.
It's just not possible to stay engaged with these difficult areas year after year after year all by yourself.
You have to have a group of people to share your struggles with.
You have to have a group of people to help you use your anger at injustice as energy to carry you forward, but to do it in a productive way.

She talked about how young people will see the injustice and get mad as hell, and it really helps to have some older people who've been around a while to help them know how to channel that energy, and not to act in a way that's either destructive or where they just burn out.
I think that's very much like our sangha.
You are here supporting my practice.
For those of you who don't know, a sangha is a Buddhist term.
It means the group of people who practice together.

So your presence here supports my practice, my presence here supports your practice, and if we have problems, either in here or out in the world, we have our Dharma friends or teachers to talk to about what's going on and how to handle it.
I don't know about you, but I don't think I could go very far or very long all by myself.
If I was just meditating at home by myself, I imagine I'd give that up before too long, or do it pretty sporadically.
So it's been really helpful to have a sangha.
We consider it one of the three treasures in Buddhism, and that's exactly what Gloria Steinem was talking about.
You've got to have company, you've got to have help.

One of the people whose writings we most appreciate is a Japanese priest from the 12th century, Eihei Dogen, and in one of his writings he talked about practicing the way: intelligence or lack of it does not matter, between the dull and the sharp-witted there is no distinction.
Buddhist practice is open to everyone, and everyone has the potential for Buddha nature, to reach their highest possibility.
There are no distinctions between social class or economic class or ethnic differences in Buddhism.
Everyone can practice.
And I think Gloria Steinem was saying the very same thing when she talked about "we are linked, not ranked."
What she meant by that is there can't be liberation for some people and not others.
Some people are not better than, or more deserving of liberation than, others.
Equality belongs to all of us.
Then there were just a couple more things she said.
She was optimistic about the future, which is always good to hear, especially from someone who's been working for as long as she has to change things.

One of the reasons she said so much has changed in her lifetime: when she was a young woman, she said, the pressure to just get married and have children was enormous, and there was hardly any other choice a young woman could make in the 1950s.

She said that if you got married in the 1950s, a woman couldn't get a credit card without her husband's permission, and if you got married you had to change your name to your husband's family name, and if you didn't want to do that you had to go to court.
These things are long gone.
So, well, there's a lot of work to do and a lot of things that are still problems, but a lot has changed, and she feels optimistic because of that.
Then someone asked her what we should do now, and she had three things that she recommended.
One of them was, every day do something outrageous.
Do at least one outrageous thing, even if that means leaving the dishes in the sink.
The other thing she said was to be a good listener.
You learn a lot more listening to people than you do talking.
And the last thing was to do, look, she called them little kindnesses, every day in your day-to-day life.
That might mean having a friendly conversation with the clerk at the store, or if you're walking down the street and you see someone carrying a bunch of packages, maybe you offer to help them.
Those little kindnesses very much remind me of a statement Suzuki Roshi made.
He's the person who founded the San Francisco Zen Center in the 1950s.

He talked about each one of us shining one corner of the world, and what he meant by that is exactly what Gloria Steinem is talking about: in your day-to-day life you have the chance to do little kind things, so do those.
He called those shining one corner of the world.
And that's the same thing that our founding teacher Norman Fischer talks about.

Whenever he ordained someone as a priest, he gives them three pieces of advice, but then he also gives the same advice, and that is: one, be humble; two, see everyone as Buddha, which means treat everyone with respect, and you can learn something from everybody, even difficult people; and the third one is, try to be helpful.
That's the same thing as a little kindness, or shining one corner of the world.
So I thought a lot of the things she talked about were very congruent with our practice, and that's what I wanted to talk about tonight.
That's the end of my talk.
I didn't bring a watch, so I don't know if we have any time.
If we have a few minutes there could be questions or comments, but if we're out of time, are we out of time?
How much have we got?
